title: Probabilistic combinatorial optimization problems
contribution: Bertsimas's 1988 MIT PhD thesis founds a priori optimization for four probabilistic combinatorial problem families (the new PMST, the PTSP, the PVRP, the TSFLP and PTSFLP): closed-form expected costs, NP-completeness of the PMST, LP-duality and combinatorial bounds, worst-case and asymptotically optimal heuristics, and sqrt(np) laws showing the a priori strategies asymptotically equivalent to re-optimization, plus a PTSP heuristic study.
problem_entry: SD+IO (HS in §3.7): re-solving a combinatorial problem on every random subset of its instance costs exponentially many NP-hard solves; optimize instead an a priori solution with a trivial update rule for expected cost and compare it with the re-optimization expectation (pp. 11-13); motives: realistic randomness and robustness of deterministic optima (p. 11); problem class inherited from Odoni's group (pp. 18, 71, 125).
key_idea: One fixed tree, tour, route or location plus tour, updated in O(n) by retracing or skipping absent nodes, is asymptotically as good as re-optimization in every problem considered (pp. 13, 26, 160); since the a priori problems are hard, use heuristics whose deterministic guarantee survives on every instance: the order-preserving spacefilling curve (pp. 99-100), the MST-induced tour (pp. 89-90), the cyclic heuristic (pp. 135-136).
assumptions: General p(S) allowed (pp. 29, 128) but most results assume independent presence, often one common p (pp. 31-32); triangle inequality for upper bounds and routing heuristics (pp. 82, 96, 131), not for LP-duality lower bounds (p. 82); symmetric distances for convenience (p. 132); random Euclidean (uniform unit square) and random-length (uniform [0,1] costs) models (pp. 53-54); plane and uniform law chosen for clarity, extensions claimed not proved (p. 146); no real data (p. 120).
proof_devices: Edge-by-edge expected length by inclusion-exclusion on 'no node present' probabilities, valid for dependent presence; product form and O(n) leaf peeling under independence (Theorems 2.1-2.2, pp. 30-32); recursion for the number of demanding customers for PVRP routes (Theorem 4.1, pp. 128-130)

NP-completeness of the PMST with unit costs and one common p by reduction from EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS, using properties of phi(k) and an exchange step (Theorem 2.4, pp. 33-38; Theorem 2.5, pp. 39-40); hardness first suspected from the p -> 0 limit, the NP-complete network design problem on a tree (pp. 38-39)
RTSP (a tour optimal on every subset) placed in Sigma_2^P, and in co-NP for distinct edge-set costs (Proposition 3.12, p. 93)

Optimal value as a function of the coverage probability p (continuity, monotonicity, concavity or piecewise convexity, both limits) and bounds from concavity (Propositions 2.6-2.7, 3.5; pp. 40-42, 84-85)

Tightness by explicit example: the MST as a PMST solution is off by O(n) as p -> 0 and the bound is best possible (Proposition 2.8, pp. 43-44); star example where MST re-optimization loses to the a priori tree for np < 3 (pp. 47-48)
Exchange arguments for polynomial special cases: star trees (Theorems 2.11, 2.13, 2.14, pp. 49-53); the constant PTSP (Proposition 3.11, p. 91)
Cycle-structure comparison of the optimal tour with the tour that skips one point, closing Jaillet's n-prime condition for odd n without the triangle inequality (Proposition 3.1, pp. 78-80)

LP duality: node potentials subtracted from distances, nonnegative reduced costs, dual = transportation problem, giving lower bounds for the PTSP and both PVRP strategies (Propositions 3.2, 4.5; pp. 80-82, 134-135)

Steele's subadditive Euclidean functionals with always-present 'black' representatives for subadditivity, Chernoff concentration of the number present, size-only instance cost, and a p -> 1 sandwich identifying beta*sqrt(p) (Theorems 2.15-2.16, 3.19; pp. 55-63, 102-104); Frieze's zeta(3) for random lengths (Theorems 2.17-2.18, pp. 64-66)

Worst-case ratios: c/p-type bound for TSP heuristics balanced against an np-order bound to give O(sqrt n) (Propositions 3.14-3.15, Theorem 3.16, pp. 97-98); O(log n) for the spacefilling curve (Theorem 3.17, pp. 99-100); 2d for MST-induced tours (Theorem 3.10, p. 90); PVRP constant and Q+1 (Theorems 4.10-4.11, pp. 139-140); 1/2(1-p_i*) for the TSFLP heuristic (Theorem 5.4, p. 153)
Lower bound on re-optimization from nearest-neighbour labels via Rosenkrantz et al.'s lemma and Jensen's inequality (Proposition 3.13, pp. 94-96)
Regime split of PVRP asymptotics by the growth of capacity against sqrt(n), radial versus local term, with the boundary regime left uncovered (Theorems 4.12-4.14, pp. 141-146; p. 143)
Average-case analysis of a failing heuristic: nearest neighbour gives expected PTSP length about p(1-p)n/2 under random lengths while re-optimization stays bounded (Theorem 3.22, pp. 107-109)
experiments: Euclidean PTSP only (§3.7, Louis Howell credited, p. 4): spacefilling curve (O(n log n), 5,000 nodes), 2-opt and 3-opt, 2-p-opt with auxiliary matrices, 1-shift with best-improvement, angular sorting; 10 random 100-node instances averaged, E[L]/sqrt(np) read against beta_TSP ~ .765 with a random-tour floor; convergence runs n = 25-200 and an n = 100 vs 500 test of TSP tours (pp. 110-123). 'Usually optimal' judged by convergence from every start; limits printed (time and memory beyond a few hundred nodes, uncertain 3-opt threshold, angular sorting doubted); no timings, machine, real data or certificates; the conclusion's 5% figure (p. 161) has no number in §3.7.
positioning: Joins Euclidean probabilistic analysis (Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley, Karp, Steele) and random-length analysis (Karp, Frieze, Steele, Walkup) to the 'very sparse' PCOP literature (Jaillet; Jaillet-Odoni) (pp. 17-18); stochastic-programming VRPs set aside as differently defined (pp. 18-19, 124); sharpens Jaillet (pp. 72, 78-80, 102-104); improves and criticizes Berman-Simchi-Levi, whose 1988a work already treated the PTSFLP for a given tour (pp. 148, 150-156); hinges three results on Platzman-Bartholdi's O(1) conjecture (pp. 100-101, 164-165).
writing: Chapters 2-4 share one order (definition, roadmap, applications, closed form, complexity, properties, asymptotics, heuristics); 'surprising' ten times; numbered conjectures beside theorems; hedges on the experiments; conclusions stronger than the body (random-length 'better' where 'at least as good' is proved, pp. 54, 66, 161; 25% from a simulated constant, pp. 105, 159; 5% without a number, p. 161); 'excellent potential' (p. 165).
limits_future: Limits: O(log n), not O(1), for the spacefilling curve (pp. 100-101); even n open (p. 80); one capacity regime uncovered (p. 143); superpolynomial partitioning (pp. 106-107); time and memory beyond a few hundred nodes (p. 120); Steiner strategy unanalysed for random lengths (pp. 66-67). Future: probabilistic shortest path, assignment and m-PTSP (pp. 162-164); prove the O(1) conjecture, an O(c^n) PTSP algorithm, O(1) heuristics for PTSP and PMST (pp. 164-165). The O(1) hinge was refuted by Bertsimas and Grigni in 1989 (S038 p. 10; S161).

method_links.note: Formulation first (the re-solve chore becomes one a priori expected-cost problem), a dual device (LP duality to a transportation problem for lower bounds, 'a mathematical programming rather than a combinatorial approach') and a printed boundary (NP-completeness, Sigma_2^P, O(log n) against a conjectured O(1), open problems) are present in 1988, earlier than the 1993-1995 evidence the SKILL cites. Class preservation is reversed: the probabilistic MST leaves the greedy-solvable class and the thesis prices that loss instead of changing the device; no solve times are measured for the hard problems.

The property is the robustness and globality of an a priori solution, priced in tractability (p. 29) and in ratios indexed by the coverage probability p, with the bad case p -> 0 printed and shown tight (pp. 43-44, 97); the optimal value is drawn as a curve in p. The knob is a model parameter, not a protection level chosen by a decision-maker, and there is no violation bound. [inferred] The 1988 price of robustness predates The price of robustness (2004); no text links them.

Spacefilling-curve tours warm-start 2-p-opt and 1-shift, and the deterministic incumbent (TSP tours) is dueled on the stochastic objective at two sizes, the larger reversing the small-n verdict. No exact solve or certificate: 'usually optimal' rests on convergence from every start, and the conclusion's 'within 5%' has no number in §3.7 (an early Tension T1). Out of memory beyond a few hundred nodes, the study falls back on the sorting heuristic (a loose analogue of Heuristic 3).

Strategies are judged by expected cost against the re-optimization ideal, not an owner's current rule, and applications are motivations without data. Operator priorities define the strategies (network structure unchanged; the same vehicle and driver), and Chapter 5 rejects a heuristic that gives the planner a location without its cost, replacing it with one that returns an operating tour for every instance and its expected cost.

Lineage step only: the problem class came from Odoni's group (Jaillet's 1985 thesis, Odoni's mail-delivery PTSP, the Jaillet-Odoni PVRP), documenting the origin the SKILL marks [inferred] for 1985-1995; the thesis's extensions and open problems seed S038, S148 and S161. Gate, course, book and company steps are not visible.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a priori solution with a cheap update rule, priced against re-solving
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The thesis is the origin of the framing: one tree, tour, route or location plus tour, updated in O(n), judged by expected cost against re-optimization in the worst case and asymptotically, for all four problem families; recurs in S038, S017 and S148.
sqrt(np) laws with identified constants (beta_MST, beta_TSP) for a priori and re-optimization strategies, and a regime split of the PVRP asymptotics by capacity growth.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry deterministic devices into the stochastic version and measure what survives
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tree doubling and the constant TSP survive; TSP-heuristic guarantees weaken with p; non-crossing of optimal tours and Held-Karp dynamic programming fail, so Karp's partitioning loses polynomial time.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: print the looseness of your own constants and the conjecture that would close it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: O(log n) proved and O(1) conjectured, with three results hinged on it; the 1.15 Steiner ratio; Conjecture 2.20 for the random-length constant; open problems listed. The O(1) hinge was refuted by Bertsimas and Grigni in 1989 (S161).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: tightness audit of one's own bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The bound on the MST used as a PMST solution is shown best possible by an explicit complete-graph example; recurs in S148.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic optimality as the warrant for a simple heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The cyclic heuristic started from any O(sqrt n) tour is asymptotically optimal for PVRP strategy a under constant or slowly growing capacity; Berman and Simchi-Levi's location heuristic is asymptotically optimal; the optimal PTSP tour solves PVRP strategy b asymptotically when capacity grows fast.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: probe the knob's limits to locate hardness and structure
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: As p -> 0 the PMST objective tends to the NP-complete network design problem on a tree, the observation that 'originally led us to suspect' hardness before the reduction; both limits frame the value curves; near-starlike low-p tours suggested angular sorting.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: scale test of whether the stochastic model is needed (false-alarm check)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: TSP tours look surprisingly good on the PTSP at n = 100, which would make the PTSP pointless; rerun at n = 500 they degrade with n, so the small-n result masked the gap.

transferable: For a problem re-solved on many perturbed instances, optimize the deployment rule (an a priori solution and a trivial update) for expected cost and compare it with the re-solve ideal both in the worst case and asymptotically (pp. 12-13, 160).

Write an expectation over 2^n instances edge by edge, each edge's cost times the probability it is used, by inclusion-exclusion on 'no node present' events (covers dependent presence); order the sum by peeling leaves to make it linear-time (pp. 30-32).

To guess whether a parametrized problem is hard, push the parameter to its limits and see which known problem appears (p -> 0 gives network design on a tree); then prove hardness by a reduction with an exchange step (pp. 33-39).

Lower-bound a combinatorial expected cost by LP duality: subtract node potentials from the distances, keep reduced costs nonnegative and maximize; the dual is a transportation problem and needs no triangle inequality (pp. 80-82, 134-135).

For a sqrt(np) law: show an instance's expected cost depends only on how many nodes are present, concentrate that number with a Chernoff bound, then pin the constant with sandwich bounds as p -> 1 (pp. 55-63, 102-104).
When a capacity can grow with n, split the asymptotics by its growth against sqrt(n) (radial against local term) and state the regime left uncovered (pp. 141-146).

Choose the local-search neighbourhood by asking which moves are minor under the new objective (global coupling at low p makes section reversal major, so move one node), and switch to best-improvement when gains can appear anywhere (pp. 114-116).
Before claiming that the stochastic model matters, run the deterministic incumbent on it at two sizes; a small instance can hide the gap (pp. 121-123).
coauthors: none (sole-author thesis); thesis supervisors Amedeo R. Odoni and Daniel Kleitman, committee member Thomas L. Magnanti; Patrick Jaillet read the whole thesis and Louis Howell contributed to §3.7 (pp. 1, 3-4)

quotes.text: one pays for these nice properties (robustness, globality) by changing the complexity of the problem radically.
If these results were indicative of the behavior of good TSP tours on PTSP problems, then Jaillet’s bound (3.5) would seem to be a false alarm, not applicable except in contrived examples.
